Love your enemies, and do good to those who hate you: and pray for those who persecute and slander you: so that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven, who makes His sun to rise upon the good and the bad, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust. 

<margin>Enemies are to be loved.</margin>
You answer: He did not say these things to me. He said them to the apostles: He said them to the perfect. Have you not heard: "so that you may be children of your Father"? If you do not desire to be a child of God, the law does not pertain to you. Although, not even he is good who does not wish to be perfect. Take this also: if you do not desire a reward, the commandment does not pertain to you. For it follows: "For if you love those who love you, what reward will you have?" <margin>Luke 6</margin> As if He were saying, none at all. For to do that is not a virtue, but not to do it is a crime. Nothing is owed to either party when like is returned for like. 

Listen to Paul, <margin>Paul, a consultant of laws.</margin> the great consultant and interpreter of Christian laws. "Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse." <margin>Romans 12</margin> "Returning evil to no one for evil. If it is possible, so far as it depends on you, having peace with all men: not defending yourselves, dearly beloved, but give place to wrath. For it is written: Vengeance is mine, and I will repay, says the Lord." <margin>Deuteronomy 32</margin> "But if your enemy is hungry, feed him. If he is thirsty, give him a drink. For in doing this you will heap coals of fire upon his head. Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good." 

"What then will happen," you ask, "if I nourish another's insolence with my gentleness, and by enduring an old injury, I invite a new one?" <margin>It is more fitting for a Christian to suffer injuries than to cause them.</margin> If you can either escape or repel the evil without your own evil, no one forbids you from doing so; otherwise, beware of saying: "it is easier to do than to suffer." If you can, correct the person, either by overwhelming them with favors or by conquering them with mildness. If it cannot be otherwise, it is better that one should perish than both. It is better for you to grow rich through the profit of patience than for both of you to become evil through the mutual retaliation of evil. 

Therefore, let it be a Christian decree <margin>The decree of Christianity.</margin> to compete with everyone in love, mildness, and kindness; but in contention, detraction, insult, and injury, to yield willingly even to the lowest. "But he is unworthy," they say, "to have good done to him or to be yielded to." But it is worthy of you that you do it; it is worthy of Christ, for whose grace it is done. "I do not wish to harm anyone," they say, "nor will I allow myself to be harmed." <summary>Erasmus argues that the command to love one's enemies applies to all Christians, not just the perfect. He cites Paul's teachings on non-retaliation and emphasizes that it is better to suffer an injury than to return evil for evil.</summary>
